title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 59
paragraphs: However, not long after this, the followers of Megacles and those of Lycurgus joined together and drove him out. Thus Peisistratus had obtained possession of Athens for the first time, and thus he lost the power before he had it firmly rooted. But those who had driven Peisistratus out afterwards became embroiled in feud with one another again. And Megacles, harassed by the party strife, sent a message to Peisistratus asking whether he was willing to take his daughter to wife on condition of becoming tyrant. Peisistratus accepted the proposal, and when they had made an agreement on these terms, they contrived with a view to his return a device the most naive by far, as I think, that ever was practiced—especially considering that it was devised at a time when the Hellenic race had long been set apart from the barbarian as more clever and further removed from foolish simplicity, and devised among the Athenians, who are accounted the first of the Greeks in ability. In the deme of Paeania there was a woman named Phya, four cubits high all but three fingers, and also fair of form. This woman they dressed in full armor and set upon a chariot, and showed her the bearing in which she would best look the part, and so they drove to the city, having sent on heralds to run before them. When these heralds arrived at the city, they said what they had been commanded to say, speaking as follows: “Athenians, receive with favor Peisistratus, whom Athena herself, honoring him above all men, is bringing back to her Acropolis.” So the heralds went around everywhere saying this, and a report immediately reached the demes in the country round about that Athena was bringing Peisistratus back. At the same time the men of the city, convinced that the woman was the goddess herself, were paying worship to a human creature and receiving Peisistratus.
